---
title: "Population Adjustment Theory"
---

## Introduction {#sec-pat-intro}

Before any symbols, here is the problem in plain words. Chapter 14's Bucher method estimates the effect
of $A$ versus $B$ by subtracting two relative effects that share a common comparator $C$: the effect of
$A$ versus $C$ measured in one trial and the effect of $B$ versus $C$ measured in another. This
subtraction is valid only when each trial's relative effect is a fixed number that does not depend on
the patient mix. If some baseline characteristic changes the size of a treatment effect, an *effect
modifier*, and the two trials enrolled different patients, then each trial reports a relative effect
averaged over a different population, and the subtraction silently mixes the two and is biased. This
chapter is the systematic repair: instead of treating a trial's effect as a population-free constant, we
model how it depends on the covariates and re-standardize it to a population we actually care about.
That is what population adjustment means.

::: {.remark}
**Running example (anticoagulants).** We carry one clinical scenario through the whole chapter. Let $C$
be warfarin, the old common comparator; let $A$ be a new oral anticoagulant studied against warfarin in
a trial that supplies individual patient data (IPD); and let $B$ be an established direct oral
anticoagulant (DOAC) studied against warfarin in a separate trial that supplies only aggregate data
(AgD). The outcome is a major bleed within a year, so a *higher* risk is *worse*. The one covariate that
matters is old age, $X=1$ for age $75$ or over and $X=0$ otherwise, and age raises the bleeding risk on
the new drug $A$ but not on $B$ or warfarin, so age is an effect modifier of $A$ versus $C$. The $AC$
trial enrolled mostly younger patients and the $BC$ trial mostly older patients, and a reimbursement
agency wants the $A$-versus-$B$ comparison in a target population that is half older. This is exactly
the situation Bucher cannot handle and population adjustment can. We attach numbers to it in
@sec-pat-setup and return to it at every definition and theorem. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Chapter 14 left us with a clean estimator and a fragile assumption. Bucher's anchored indirect
comparison $\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}$ is unbiased for the cross-study contrast precisely when
the relative effects are constant across the trial populations (@thm-bucher-unbiased,
@def-constancy-relative-effects), and Chapter 16 showed exactly how that constancy breaks: an effect
modifier (@def-effect-modifier) whose distribution differs between the trials makes each trial report a
different marginal contrast, and the Bucher subtraction then mixes populations and is biased
(@thm-failure-of-bucher). This chapter is the systematic response to that failure. It is the conceptual
center of the book.

The idea of **population adjustment** is to refuse to treat a trial's reported effect as a
population-free constant, and instead to model how the effect depends on the covariates and to
re-standardize it to a chosen target population. Doing so requires more than aggregate trial summaries.
It requires, for at least one trial, the **individual patient data** (IPD): the covariate vector,
treatment, and outcome of each enrolled subject. The other trials may contribute only **aggregate data**
(AgD): arm-level event counts, means, and covariate summaries. A **population-adjusted indirect
comparison** (PAIC) combines an IPD trial with one or more AgD trials to deliver an effect estimate valid
in a stated target population. The methods that do this concretely, matching-adjusted indirect comparison
(MAIC, Chapter 18), simulated treatment comparison (STC, Chapter 19), and multilevel network
meta-regression (ML-NMR, Chapter 20), all rest on a single body of theory, and that theory is the subject
of the present chapter.

The central question is: **under what conditions is a population-adjusted indirect comparison
consistent for its target estimand?** The modern answer, which we follow, has two features that distinguish
it from older formulations. First, the conditions are **scale-specific**. The effect modification, the
collapsibility, and the reported effect measure each live on a scale, and whether adjustment succeeds
depends on how those scales relate. We must distinguish the model link $g$ (the scale on which the outcome
model is built and on which effect modification is defined, @def-link-function) from the reporting scale
$h$ (the scale of the effect measure actually quoted to a decision maker). When $h\circ g^{-1}$ is the
identity the scales are **aligned** (@def-scale-alignment); when they are not, adjustment that works on
$g$ need not work on $h$. Second, the classical "if and only if" statements of the early literature are
replaced by **scale-specific sufficient conditions together with a class-wise necessity** result. By *class-wise* we mean the necessity holds across a whole class of
data-generating mechanisms, not that every single mechanism in it is biased; a specific trial might
escape bias by numerical coincidence. The
"iff" is technically false for non-collapsible marginal estimands such as the odds ratio and hazard ratio,
because of non-collapsibility (@def-non-collapsibility, @thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr): even a perfectly
adjusted comparison can fail to transport a marginal odds ratio across populations. We make all of this
precise.

The development is organized around the two architectures of indirect comparison inherited from
Chapter 14. The **anchored** setup has a common comparator: an IPD trial of $A$ versus $C$ and an AgD trial
of $B$ versus $C$, with the shared arm $C$ available to absorb study-level baseline differences. The
**unanchored** setup has no common comparator: a single-arm or otherwise disconnected source of $A$ and a
disconnected source of $B$, with no shared arm to difference against. The two architectures demand
different assumptions. The anchored case needs only that the **relative** effect transports at the
conditional level (@def-conditional-constancy-relative, E.4) and that imbalanced **effect modifiers** be
adjusted (@thm-anchored-paic-consistency, E.6a to E.6e). The unanchored case needs that the **absolute**
conditional outcome transports (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute, E.5) and that imbalanced
**prognostic variables as well as** effect modifiers be adjusted (@thm-unanchored-paic-consistency, E.7),
because there is no common comparator to cancel the prognostic terms. The chapter closes with the **shared
effect modifier assumption** that makes small networks identifiable (@def-sema, E.8;
@thm-shared-em-identifiability, E.9), the scale dependence of effect modifier status as an explicit
counterexample (@exm-scale-dependence-em, E.10), the question of which parts of these assumptions are
testable from data (@prp-testable-untestable-constancy, E.11), and the definition of the target-population
estimands themselves via the g-formula (@thm-target-population-estimand, E.12). This chapter owns results
E.4 to E.12 of the proof catalogue; it builds on E.0 to E.3 from Chapters 11, 12, and 16, and on the
identification machinery of Chapters 9 and 10. A warning threads through all of it and is worth stating
at the outset: in a two-study comparison the core constancy assumptions cannot be tested from the data,
and must be defended by domain knowledge and sensitivity analysis (@sec-pat-testable).

## Data structures, models, and estimands {#sec-pat-setup}

We retain the potential-outcome framework of Chapter 9. A population $\mathcal P$ is a distribution over
covariates $X\in\mathcal X$ with density $f_{\mathcal P}$, and the conditional mean potential outcome
under treatment $t$ is $\mu_t^{\mathcal P}(x)=\mathbb E_{\mathcal P}[Y(t)\mid X=x]$. Throughout we assume
the within-trial identification conditions of Chapter 9: SUTVA and consistency (@def-sutva,
@thm-consistency-identity), within-trial conditional exchangeability (@def-ignorability), and
within-trial positivity (@def-positivity), so that each trial's conditional means are identified from its
own data by the g-formula (@thm-g-computation-unbiased). For a treatment $t$ and a population $\mathcal P$
the **marginal mean** is
$$
m_t(\mathcal P)\;=\;\int_{\mathcal X}\mu_t(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx,
$$ {#eq-pat-marginal-mean}
the same quantity written $\bar\mu_{t(\mathcal P)}$ in Chapter 14; we drop the bar here and write
$m_t(\mathcal P)$ throughout, so the reader need not carry two names for one object.

For orientation, the table below collects the symbols this chapter leans on most heavily. A reader who
keeps it in view will find the theorem statements much easier to parse; the two estimands
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg}}$ and $\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}$ are defined formally in @sec-pat-estimand-scales and
consolidated in @sec-pat-estimands.

| Symbol | Reads as |
|---|---|
| $\mathcal P_{AC},\mathcal P_{BC}$ | covariate distributions of the $AC$ trial (IPD) and the $BC$ trial (AgD) |
| $\mathcal P^{*}$, $f_{*}$ | the target population and its covariate density |
| $g$ | the model link: the scale the outcome model is fitted on (for logistic regression, the logit) |
| $h$ | the reporting scale: the scale of the effect measure quoted to a decision maker |
| $\mu_t(x)$ | conditional mean outcome (for a binary outcome, the risk) under treatment $t$ at covariates $x$ |
| $\tau^g_{ab}(x)$ | conditional contrast of $b$ versus $a$ at $x$ on scale $g$ (sign convention in @sec-pat-model) |
| $m_t(\mathcal P)$ | marginal (population-average) mean outcome under $t$ in population $\mathcal P$ |
| $\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},h}_{ab}$ | marginal effect: contrast of the transformed marginal means |
| $\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},h}_{ab}$ | population-average conditional effect: average of the stratum contrasts |
| $\theta^{\mathrm{anch}}_{AB},\theta^{\mathrm{unanch}}_{AB}$ | the anchored and unanchored PAIC estimands |
| $\tilde d_{kC(\mathcal P_j)}$ | trial $j$'s reported average conditional contrast of $k$ versus $C$ |

::: {.remark}
**Running example, with numbers.** Give the anticoagulant scenario the conditional risks that the
capstone example @exm-pat-anchored will reuse, with $X=1$ for age $75$ or over:

| $x$ | $\mu_A(x)$ (new drug) | $\mu_B(x)$ (DOAC) | $\mu_C(x)$ (warfarin) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0$ (younger) | $0.20$ | $0.30$ | $0.40$ |
| $1$ (older) | $0.50$ | $0.30$ | $0.40$ |

The bleeding risk on the new drug $A$ jumps from $0.20$ to $0.50$ with age, while $B$ and warfarin stay
flat, so age modifies $A$ versus $C$ but not $B$ versus $C$. The IPD trial enrolled $\Pr_{AC}(X=1)=0.25$
older patients, the AgD trial $\Pr_{BC}(X=1)=0.75$, and the target population has $\Pr_{*}(X=1)=0.50$.
Every definition below can be read against this one table. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#def-pat-data-structures}
## Individual patient data and aggregate data
A trial $j$ provides **individual patient data** (IPD) if its data set is the empirical distribution of
the per-subject triples $(x_i,t_i,y_i)$, so that the conditional mean function $x\mapsto\mu_t^{(j)}(x)$ is
estimable on the trial's covariate support. A trial provides **aggregate data** (AgD) if only arm-level
summaries are available: for each arm, an outcome summary (for binary outcomes an event count $r$ out of
$n$, equivalently $\hat m_t=r/n$) and covariate summaries (typically the covariate means $\bar x_j$ and
possibly higher moments), but not the per-subject records. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The asymmetry between IPD and AgD is the entire operational difficulty of population adjustment. From IPD
one can recompute the trial's effect under any target covariate distribution, because one holds the
conditional mean function. From AgD one holds only the effect already aggregated over the trial's own
covariate distribution, which one cannot re-standardize without an extra modeling assumption.

### The two architectures {#sec-pat-architectures}

The two setups differ only in whether a shared arm connects the treatments, but that one difference
drives every assumption in the chapter. The picture drawn in health-technology-assessment courses is a
network of treatments joined by trials:

```
   ANCHORED  (shared comparator C)        UNANCHORED  (no shared arm)

        A ------ C ------ B                   A            B
      IPD: A vs C  B vs C: AgD             IPD or       AgD
                                           single arm   source
      one connected network               two disconnected pieces
      target estimand: A vs B in P*        target estimand: A vs B in P*
```

In the anchored network a path runs from $A$ to $B$ through the shared node $C$; in the unanchored
network $A$ and $B$ sit in separate pieces with no path between them.

::: {#def-pat-setups}
## The anchored and unanchored setups
The **anchored two-study setup** consists of an IPD trial in population $\mathcal P_{AC}$ comparing $A$
with a common comparator $C$, and an AgD trial in population $\mathcal P_{BC}$ comparing $B$ with the same
comparator $C$. The target estimand is a contrast of $A$ versus $B$ in a target population
$\mathcal P^{*}$.

The **unanchored two-study setup** consists of a source of outcome data on $A$ (typically an IPD single
arm or trial) and a separate source of outcome data on $B$ (typically AgD), with **no common comparator**:
the two evidence sources share no treatment arm. The target estimand is again a contrast of $A$ versus $B$
in $\mathcal P^{*}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The same distinction, laid out as a table, previews the entire chapter. Read it now and refer back as
each row is proved.

| Question | Anchored: $AC$ and $BC$ trials share $C$ | Unanchored: no shared arm |
|---|---|---|
| Data available | IPD on one arm pair, AgD on another, sharing $C$ | separate sources for $A$ and for $B$ |
| What is transported | the *relative* effect (a contrast) | the *absolute* conditional outcome (each arm) |
| Assumption needed | conditional constancy of relative effects (@def-conditional-constancy-relative) | conditional constancy of absolute effects (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute) |
| Must be adjusted | imbalanced *effect modifiers* only | imbalanced effect modifiers *and* prognostic variables |
| What the comparator cancels | study baseline and purely prognostic terms | nothing: there is no comparator |
| Why it can fail | an imbalanced effect modifier omitted from $X$ | any imbalanced predictor of outcome omitted from $X$ |

In the running anticoagulant example the anchored setup is the realistic one: both the new drug $A$ and
the DOAC $B$ were trialed against warfarin $C$, so warfarin is the shared arm that absorbs how sick each
trial's patients were at baseline. An unanchored version would arise only if, say, $A$ had been licensed
on a single-arm study with no control group, leaving nothing to difference against; we treat that harder
case in @sec-pat-unanchored.

In the anchored setup the comparator $C$ plays exactly the role it played in Chapter 14: differencing each
trial's arms against $C$ removes the study-specific baseline (@prp-baseline-cancellation in Chapter 14).
Population adjustment then repairs the *residual* bias from effect-modifier imbalance that survives that
cancellation. In the unanchored setup there is no comparator to difference against, so the baseline itself
must be modeled and transported, which is a far stronger demand. The rest of the chapter quantifies that
difference.

### The conditional outcome model {#sec-pat-model}

All of the methods specialize a single regression model, the network meta-regression of @dias2018nma,
written on the model link $g$. With $C$ as the reference treatment, the linear predictor for an individual
with covariates $x$ on arm $k$ in study $j$ is
$$
\eta_{jk}(x)\;=\;g\!\left(\mu_k^{(j)}(x)\right)\;=\;\mu_j+\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top x+\gamma_k+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}^\top x,
\qquad \gamma_C=0,\ \boldsymbol\beta_{2,C}=\mathbf 0,
$$ {#eq-pat-nmr}
in the notation of [Notation](/notation.qmd): $\mu_j$ is the study baseline, $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ the
prognostic main effects, $\gamma_k$ the treatment main effect of $k$ versus $C$, and $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$
the treatment-by-covariate interactions of $k$ versus $C$.

To see @eq-pat-nmr in the flesh, put the anticoagulant trial into it on the logit link
$g=\operatorname{logit}$, with the single covariate $x=\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{age}\ge 75\}$. The warfarin arm
of the IPD trial has linear predictor $\eta_{AC,C}(x)=\mu_{AC}+\beta_1 x$; the new-drug arm adds the
treatment main effect and its age interaction, $\eta_{AC,A}(x)=\mu_{AC}+\beta_1 x+\gamma_A+\beta_{2,A}\,x$.
Here $\mu_{AC}$ sets the baseline log-odds of bleeding on warfarin among younger patients, $\beta_1$ says
how age alone shifts that log-odds, $\gamma_A$ is the log-odds change from switching to the new drug at
$x=0$, and $\beta_{2,A}$ is the extra log-odds change from switching among older patients, that is, the
effect modification by age. A nonzero $\beta_{2,A}$ is exactly what makes age an effect modifier of $A$
versus $C$ on the logit scale.

By @lem-emcoll-interaction the conditional
effect of an active treatment $k$ versus the comparator $C$ on scale $g$ is the linear-in-$x$ contrast
$$
\tau^{g}_{kC}(x)\;=\;g\!\left(\mu_C(x)\right)-g\!\left(\mu_k(x)\right)\;=\;-\bigl(\gamma_k+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}^\top x\bigr),
$$ {#eq-pat-tau-linear}
using the reference-second index convention of Chapter 14, so that $\tau^{g}_{kC}(x)$ is the conditional
analogue of the trial contrast $d_{kC}=\eta_C-\eta_k$ and a positive value means $k$ improves the (worse
is larger) outcome relative to $C$. The minus sign appears because $\gamma_k$ in @eq-pat-nmr is the shift
of $k$ relative to $C$, whereas $\tau^g_{kC}$ measures $C$ relative to $k$. The covariate component $X_\ell$ is an effect modifier of $k$ versus
$C$ on scale $g$ if and only if its interaction coefficient $\beta_{2,k,\ell}$ is nonzero
(@lem-emcoll-interaction).

::: {.remark}
**Sign convention, read this once.** We follow Chapter 14's reference-second convention: the second
subscript names the reference treatment. So $\tau^g_{kC}(x)=g(\mu_C(x))-g(\mu_k(x))$ subtracts the
active-treatment term from the comparator term, and because the outcome is "worse is larger" (a bleed, a
death), a **positive** $\tau^g_{kC}$ means treatment $k$ is **better** than $C$: it lowers the bad
outcome. This is the opposite of the naive "$k$ minus $C$" reading, and every number in the worked
examples depends on it. One line to memorize: a positive contrast means the first-named treatment wins.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

We do not require the linear form @eq-pat-nmr for the abstract theorems below;
they hold for an arbitrary conditional mean model, with @eq-pat-nmr used only when we need explicit
parameters (for the shared effect modifier assumption and for the worked example).

### The two estimand scales {#sec-pat-estimand-scales}

Chapter 11 introduced the two population-level effects that a single scale admits, and we will need both.

The difference between these two is the subtlest idea in the chapter, so meet it first with numbers. Take
two equally sized strata, younger and older, with bleeding risk under drug $b$ of $0.30$ in both and under
drug $a$ of $0.20$ (young) and $0.50$ (old). The **marginal** way pools first: the population risk under
$b$ is $0.30$ and under $a$ is $0.35$, and it contrasts those two pooled numbers. The **conditional** way
contrasts first: the effect is $0.30-0.20=0.10$ among the young and $0.30-0.50=-0.20$ among the old, and
it averages those two effects to $-0.05$. On the risk-difference scale these happen to agree ($-0.05$
either way); on the odds-ratio scale they will not, and that gap is the whole story of non-collapsibility
below. Keep the slogan: **marginal pools then contrasts; conditional contrasts then pools**.

On a reporting scale $h$, in population $\mathcal P$, the **marginal effect** (@def-marginal-effect) is the
contrast of the transformed marginal means,
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},h}_{ab}(\mathcal P)\;=\;h\!\left(m_b(\mathcal P)\right)-h\!\left(m_a(\mathcal P)\right),
$$ {#eq-pat-marg}
and the **population-average conditional effect** (@def-conditional-effect) is the average of the
stratum-specific contrasts,
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},h}_{ab}(\mathcal P)\;=\;\int_{\mathcal X}\Bigl[h\!\left(\mu_b(x)\right)-h\!\left(\mu_a(x)\right)\Bigr]f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx
\;=\;\int_{\mathcal X}\tau^{h}_{ab}(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx .
$$ {#eq-pat-cond}
When $h$ is the identity the two coincide for every population, because the link passes through the
integral; for a nonlinear $h$ they differ in general by Jensen's inequality, the **collapsibility gap** of
@def-collapsibility (this is catalogue E.0). The marginal effect answers "what happens to the population
mean outcome if everyone switches from $a$ to $b$"; the conditional effect answers "what is the average
within-stratum effect." Both are legitimate, they answer different questions, and the theorems below are
careful to say which one a given method recovers.

The two scales that recur, the model link $g$ and the reporting scale $h$, are easy to confuse because a
health researcher meets them as named effect measures, not as functions. The cheat sheet below maps the
common measures to their roles and flags where the chapter's caveats bite.

| Named measure | Model link $g$ | Reporting scale $h$ | Collapsible? | Caveat that bites |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Risk difference | identity | identity | yes, directly | none: adjustment recovers the marginal effect |
| Risk ratio | log | log | yes, if contrast constant | mild: needs a constant conditional contrast |
| Odds ratio | logit | logit | no | part (c): only the *conditional* odds ratio is recovered |
| Hazard ratio | log-hazard | log-hazard | no | part (c): only the *conditional* hazard ratio is recovered |
| Mean survival (RMST) | log-hazard | time scale | scale misaligned | part (d): balancing on $g$ need not deliver $h$ |

Two grades of collapsibility appear in the table. A measure is *directly* collapsible if the marginal and
conditional effects coincide for *every* covariate distribution (the risk difference), and merely
*collapsible* if they coincide only *when the conditional contrast is constant* across strata (the risk
ratio). The non-collapsible rows, the odds ratio and hazard ratio, are where "adjust perfectly and still
read off a population-specific number" happens; the last row, where $h$ is not even $g$, is scale
misalignment.

We abbreviate the trial's reported average conditional
contrast, following Chapter 16, by
$$
\tilde d_{kC(\mathcal P_j)}\;=\;\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{kC}(\mathcal P_j)\;=\;\int\tau^{g}_{kC}(x)\,f_j(x)\,dx .
$$ {#eq-pat-trial-contrast}

::: {#def-pat-imbalance}
## Balance and the adjustment set
A covariate (or covariate component) is **balanced** across two populations if it has the same
distribution in both, and **imbalanced** otherwise. The **adjustment set** $X$ of a PAIC is the collection
of covariates that the method measures and balances or regresses on; covariates outside $X$ are
**unadjusted**. We write the full covariate as $(X,W)$ when we wish to single out an unadjusted component
$W$, and call $W$ balanced when its conditional distribution given $X$ is the same in both populations.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Conditional constancy of relative effects {#sec-pat-ccre}

The assumption that licenses an anchored comparison is that the *conditional* relative effect is the same
quantity in the trial population and in the target. This differs from the marginal constancy of
Chapter 14, and it is exactly the structural invariance that Chapter 12 required for transportability.

::: {#def-conditional-constancy-relative}
## Conditional constancy of relative effects (anchored)
Two populations $\mathcal P_1,\mathcal P_2$ satisfy **conditional constancy of relative effects on scale
$g$ with respect to $X$**, for the treatment pair $(a,b)$, if the conditional effect @eq-emcoll-cate is the
same function of $x$ in both populations on the common covariate support:
$$
\tau^{\mathcal P_1,g}_{ab}(x)\;=\;\tau^{\mathcal P_2,g}_{ab}(x)\qquad\text{for all }x .
$$ {#eq-pat-ccre}
Equivalently, the conditional contrast $\tau^{g}_{ab}(\cdot)$ is a population-free function. (Corresponds
to E.4 in the proof catalogue.) $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Conditional constancy says the treatment effect *at a fixed patient profile* is a
property of the drug, not of who happened to enroll. In the anticoagulant example it asks that the
age-specific risk difference of the new drug versus warfarin, $0.20$ among the young and $-0.10$ among the
old, be the same numbers in the $AC$ trial, in the $BC$ trial, and in the target. What is allowed to
differ between populations is the *mix* of young and old; what must not differ is the effect *within* each
age group. Chapter 14's marginal constancy instead demands that the population-averaged effect itself be
identical; conditional constancy is what lets us re-standardize a trial to a new patient mix.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Conditional versus marginal constancy.** Constancy of *marginal* relative effects
(@def-constancy-relative-effects) asserts that the population-level number $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ is the same
in every population. Conditional constancy @eq-pat-ccre asserts only that the per-stratum contrast
$\tau^g_{ab}(x)$ is the same; the marginal effect may still differ across populations because it averages
the same $\tau^g_{ab}(\cdot)$ against different covariate densities. Neither assumption implies the other.
Under conditional constancy the population-average conditional effects @eq-pat-cond agree only if the
covariate distributions agree or the contrast is constant in $x$; conversely, equal marginal effects can
arise from different conditional contrasts that happen to average to the same number. Conditional constancy is the natural assumption for population
adjustment precisely because it permits the marginal effect to vary with the population while pinning down
the mechanism that generates that variation. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Conditional constancy is the hypothesis that makes the trial's conditional model portable. The next
proposition records the consequence we will use repeatedly: under @eq-pat-ccre the population-average
conditional effect in any target is identified from the source conditional contrast and the target
covariate distribution, by the transport g-formula of Chapter 12.

::: {#prp-pat-conditional-transport}
## Conditional effects transport under conditional constancy
Suppose conditional constancy of relative effects on scale $g$ (@def-conditional-constancy-relative) holds
from a source population $\mathcal P$ to a target $\mathcal P^{*}$, with target support contained in the
source support (overlap, equivalently the positivity condition of @def-positivity). Then the source
conditional contrast $\tau^g_{ab}(\cdot)$,
identified within the source by the g-formula (@thm-g-computation-unbiased), determines the target
population-average conditional effect by the transport g-formula (@thm-conditional-transportability):
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})\;=\;\int_{\mathcal X}\tau^g_{ab}(x)\,f_{\mathcal P^{*}}(x)\,dx
\;=\;\mathbb E_{X\sim\mathcal P}\!\left[\,w(X)\,\tau^g_{ab}(X)\,\right],\qquad
w(x)=\frac{f_{\mathcal P^{*}}(x)}{f_{\mathcal P}(x)} .
$$ {#eq-pat-cond-transport}
:::

::: {.proof}
By conditional constancy the function $\tau^g_{ab}(\cdot)$ identified in the source equals the
corresponding function in the target on the common support. The target population-average conditional
effect is by definition @eq-pat-cond the expectation of this function under $f_{\mathcal P^{*}}$, which is
the first equality. For the second, change measure from the target density to the source density: wherever
$f_{\mathcal P}(x)>0$ we have $f_{\mathcal P^{*}}(x)=w(x)f_{\mathcal P}(x)$, and overlap guarantees the
target support is covered, so
$\int\tau^g_{ab}(x)f_{\mathcal P^{*}}(x)\,dx=\int\tau^g_{ab}(x)w(x)f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx
=\mathbb E_{X\sim\mathcal P}[w(X)\tau^g_{ab}(X)]$. This is the reweighting form @eq-transport-gformula of the
transport g-formula applied to the integrand $\tau^g_{ab}$, which is itself a fixed function of $x$
constructed from the source conditional means. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, and why the density ratio is legitimate.** This proposition is the workhorse of the
chapter: it says an effect measured in one population can be recomputed for another just by reweighting.
The reweighting step rewards a slow reading. In the discrete case it is elementary. Suppose the covariate
takes finitely many values; then $\int\tau^g_{ab}(x)f_{\mathcal P^{*}}(x)\,dx$ is the sum
$\sum_x\tau^g_{ab}(x)f_{\mathcal P^{*}}(x)$, and multiplying and dividing each term by $f_{\mathcal P}(x)$
rewrites it as $\sum_x[f_{\mathcal P^{*}}(x)/f_{\mathcal P}(x)]\,\tau^g_{ab}(x)f_{\mathcal P}(x)$, a
source-weighted average of the same contrast with each stratum reweighted by
$w(x)=f_{\mathcal P^{*}}(x)/f_{\mathcal P}(x)$. Strata over-represented in the target get weight above
$1$; under-represented strata get weight below $1$. This is the importance-sampling (Radon-Nikodym)
identity, and it is the theoretical target that MAIC will estimate. The overlap assumption is what keeps
the weight finite: if the target puts mass where the source has none, $f_{\mathcal P}(x)=0$ makes $w(x)$
undefined, and no reweighting of source data can conjure an effect for a patient profile the source never
observed. That is the precise sense in which population adjustment transports but does not extrapolate.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The two forms of @eq-pat-cond-transport, integrating against $f_{*}$ and reweighting by $w$, are the two
faces of population adjustment. **Outcome regression** models the conditional means from IPD and averages
them over the target covariate distribution; this is STC and the regression core of ML-NMR. **Weighting**
reweights the IPD by an estimate of $w$, so that each arm's weighted mean outcome estimates
$m_t(\mathcal P^{*})=\mathbb E_{X\sim\mathcal P}[w(X)\mu_t(X)]$; this is MAIC, and contrasting its weighted
arm means gives a *marginal* effect. The remainder of the
chapter establishes when each delivers the target estimand.

## Conditional constancy of absolute effects {#sec-pat-ccae}

The unanchored setup has no comparator to difference against, so it must transport the absolute conditional
outcome, not merely the contrast. The corresponding assumption is strictly stronger.

::: {#def-conditional-constancy-absolute}
## Conditional constancy of absolute effects (unanchored)
Two populations $\mathcal P_1,\mathcal P_2$ satisfy **conditional constancy of absolute effects** with
respect to $X$ if for every treatment $t$ and every $x$ on the common support,
$$
\mu_t^{\mathcal P_1}(x)\;=\;\mu_t^{\mathcal P_2}(x) .
$$ {#eq-pat-ccae}
That is, the entire conditional mean function, arm by arm, is population-free. (Corresponds to E.5 in the
proof catalogue.) $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Absolute constancy is a far heavier promise than relative constancy: it asks that
the *actual risk* on each drug, arm by arm, at a fixed patient profile, be identical across populations,
not merely that the *gap between drugs* be identical. In the anticoagulant example it would require the
older-patient bleeding risk on warfarin to be exactly $0.40$ in every population, and likewise for every
arm. Relative constancy lets the whole risk profile float up or down between populations as long as the
treatment contrast holds; absolute constancy forbids even that. The unanchored setup needs the heavier
promise because, with no comparator arm to difference against, it must reconstruct each arm's risk from
scratch. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#prp-pat-absolute-implies-relative}
## Absolute constancy is strictly stronger than relative constancy
Conditional constancy of absolute effects (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute) implies conditional
constancy of relative effects on every scale $g$ (@def-conditional-constancy-relative), for every
treatment pair. The converse is false: there exist conditional mean functions that satisfy relative
constancy on a scale $g$ but not absolute constancy.
:::

::: {.proof}
If $\mu_t^{\mathcal P_1}(x)=\mu_t^{\mathcal P_2}(x)$ for every $t$ and $x$, then for any scale $g$ and any
pair $(a,b)$,
$\tau^{\mathcal P_1,g}_{ab}(x)=g(\mu_b^{\mathcal P_1}(x))-g(\mu_a^{\mathcal P_1}(x))
=g(\mu_b^{\mathcal P_2}(x))-g(\mu_a^{\mathcal P_2}(x))=\tau^{\mathcal P_2,g}_{ab}(x)$, which is @eq-pat-ccre.
For the converse, let the covariate be $(X,W)$ and let the absolute means depend on a component $W$ that is
not adjusted; take, for a single covariate value and on the identity scale,
$\mu_a^{\mathcal P_1}(x,w)=\mu_b^{\mathcal P_1}(x,w)=w$ and
$\mu_a^{\mathcal P_2}(x,w)=\mu_b^{\mathcal P_2}(x,w)=w+1$. Then the contrast is identically zero in both
populations, so relative constancy holds on the identity scale, while the absolute means differ by $1$, so
absolute constancy fails. $\square$
:::

The witness in the proof is the formal seed of the difference between anchored and unanchored adjustment:
a covariate can shift both arms equally, raising the baseline risk while leaving the treatment contrast
untouched, so the absolute level changes but the contrast does not. Such
a covariate is invisible to an anchored comparison and fatal to an unanchored one. We now isolate that
phenomenon as the effect-modifier-versus-prognostic distinction, which is the algebraic heart of the
chapter.

## The effect modifier versus prognostic distinction {#sec-pat-em-pv}

Recall from Chapter 11 the four-cell classification of a covariate by whether it is prognostic (affects the
conditional means, @def-prognostic-variable) and whether it is an effect modifier (affects the conditional
contrast, @def-effect-modifier). The single cell that powers anchored comparison is the **purely
prognostic** one: a covariate that moves both arms but not their contrast. We prove the two cancellation
facts that separate the anchored and unanchored architectures. Both have machine-checked counterparts in
the companion Coq development.

For a reader arriving directly at Part IV, here are the two words in one line each. A **prognostic
variable** moves the outcome under *both* arms: sicker patients bleed more whatever drug they take. An
**effect modifier** moves the *difference* between arms: the new drug's advantage over warfarin shrinks or
reverses with age. A covariate can be one, the other, both, or neither, the four cells of Chapter 11:

| | Not an effect modifier (contrast flat in it) | Effect modifier (contrast varies in it) |
|---|---|---|
| **Not prognostic** (outcome flat in it) | irrelevant: ignore it | uncommon, but must be adjusted |
| **Prognostic** (outcome varies in it) | purely prognostic: cancels when anchored | prognostic *and* modifying: always adjust |

The load-bearing cell is the lower left, purely prognostic. In the anticoagulant example, age sits in the
lower right for the $A$-versus-$C$ contrast (prognostic and a modifier), whereas a shared frailty score
that raised every arm's bleeding risk equally would sit in the lower left. The two lemmas below prove
exactly why the lower-left cell is free in an anchored comparison and fatal in an unanchored one.

::: {#lem-pat-pv-cancellation}
## Anchored cancellation of purely prognostic covariates
Let the full covariate be $(X,W)$ and fix a scale $g$ and a treatment pair $(k,C)$. Suppose $W$ is **not an
effect modifier** of $k$ versus $C$ on scale $g$, in the sense that the conditional contrast does not
depend on $w$:
$$
\tau^{g}_{kC}(x,w)\;=\;\tau^{g}_{kC}(x,w')\qquad\text{for all }x,w,w' .
$$ {#eq-pat-notem}
Then, writing $\tau^g_{kC}(x)$ for the common value, the population-average conditional contrast over any
population $\mathcal P$ depends on $\mathcal P$ only through the marginal distribution of $X$:
$$
\int\tau^g_{kC}(x,w)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x,w)\,dx\,dw\;=\;\int\tau^g_{kC}(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx .
$$ {#eq-pat-cancellation}
In particular, omitting $W$ from the adjustment set does not change the anchored estimand, whatever the
distribution of $W$ given $X$ and however imbalanced $W$ may be.
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/EffectModifiers.v`, `Theorem anchored_PV_cancellation`]

::: {.proof}
By hypothesis @eq-pat-notem the integrand $\tau^g_{kC}(x,w)$ equals the constant-in-$w$ value
$\tau^g_{kC}(x)$ for every $w$. Hence
$$
\int\tau^g_{kC}(x,w)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x,w)\,dx\,dw
=\int\tau^g_{kC}(x)\left(\int f_{\mathcal P}(x,w)\,dw\right)dx
=\int\tau^g_{kC}(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx,
$$
the inner integral being the marginal density of $X$. The right-hand side does not involve the conditional
distribution of $W$ given $X$, so it is unchanged if $W$ is left unadjusted and unchanged across
populations with different $W$-distributions. $\square$
:::

::: {#lem-pat-em-not-pv}
## A prognostic variable need not be an effect modifier
"Not an effect modifier of $k$ versus $C$" does not imply "not prognostic for $k$." Concretely, there
exist conditional mean functions $\mu_k,\mu_C$ such that the contrast $\mu_k(x,w)-\mu_C(x,w)$ is constant
in $w$ (so $W$ is not an effect modifier on the identity scale) while $\mu_k(x,w)$ depends on $w$ (so $W$
is prognostic for $k$).
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/EffectModifiers.v`, `Theorem not_EM_does_not_imply_not_PV`]

::: {.proof}
Take $\mu_k(x,w)=\mu_C(x,w)=w$. Then $\mu_k(x,w)-\mu_C(x,w)=0$ for all $w$, so $W$ is not an effect
modifier; but $\mu_k(x,w)=w$ is nonconstant in $w$, so $W$ is prognostic for $k$. In words, this $W$ is
the shared-frailty kind of covariate that raises every arm's outcome by the same amount, changing who
bleeds without changing which drug is better. The same two functions
witness that absolute constancy is strictly stronger than relative constancy
(@prp-pat-absolute-implies-relative). $\square$
:::

The contrast between @lem-pat-pv-cancellation and @lem-pat-em-not-pv is the whole story in miniature. In an
anchored comparison the estimand depends on $W$ only through the contrast $\tau^g_{kC}$, so a purely
prognostic $W$ cancels and may be ignored (@lem-pat-pv-cancellation). In an unanchored comparison the
estimand depends on the absolute means $\mu_k$ themselves, which a prognostic $W$ moves even when it
modifies no contrast (@lem-pat-em-not-pv), so it cannot be ignored. This is why the anchored case adjusts
for effect modifiers while the unanchored case must adjust for prognostic variables as well.

## The anchored consistency theorem {#sec-pat-anchored}

We now assemble the central anchored result. Define the **anchored PAIC estimand** at a target
$\mathcal P^{*}$ as the difference of the two conditional contrasts, each standardized to the target:
$$
\theta^{\mathrm{anch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})
\;:=\;\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AC}(\mathcal P^{*})-\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{BC}(\mathcal P^{*})
\;=\;\int\tau^g_{AC}(x)\,f_{*}(x)\,dx-\int\tau^g_{BC}(x)\,f_{*}(x)\,dx .
$$ {#eq-pat-anchored-estimand}
On a directly collapsible scale it equals the marginal contrast that MAIC and marginal STC target; on a
non-collapsible scale those methods target the marginal contrast instead (part (c) below), and ML-NMR can
deliver either. In the two-study MAIC special case one takes $\mathcal P^{*}=\mathcal P_{BC}$, so that the
$BC$ contrast is reported directly and only the $AC$ contrast is re-standardized. The first lemma is
pure algebra and is the conditional analogue of Bucher's additivity (@lem-relative-effect-algebra). It
looks trivial, but it is the linchpin of the anchored architecture: it is the reason that subtracting two
separately re-standardized contrasts yields the correct $A$-versus-$B$ answer, and it holds pointwise on
every scale.

::: {#lem-pat-conditional-additivity}
## Pointwise additivity of conditional contrasts
For every $x$ and every scale $g$, the conditional contrasts obey
$$
\tau^g_{AB}(x)\;=\;\tau^g_{AC}(x)-\tau^g_{BC}(x).
$$ {#eq-pat-cond-additivity}
Consequently, for any population $\mathcal P$, the population-average conditional effects obey
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P)=\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AC}(\mathcal P)-\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{BC}(\mathcal P)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Using the reference-second convention $\tau^g_{ab}(x)=g(\mu_b(x))-g(\mu_a(x))$ of @eq-emcoll-cate,
$$
\tau^g_{AC}(x)-\tau^g_{BC}(x)=\bigl[g(\mu_C(x))-g(\mu_A(x))\bigr]-\bigl[g(\mu_C(x))-g(\mu_B(x))\bigr]
=g(\mu_B(x))-g(\mu_A(x))=\tau^g_{AB}(x),
$$
the comparator term $g(\mu_C(x))$ canceling pointwise. Integrating both sides against $f_{\mathcal P}$ and
using linearity of the integral (@eq-pat-cond) gives the population-average statement. $\square$
:::

Before the theorem, here is the plan in words, because the statement below has five parts that are easy to
conflate. Part (a) is the good news and does the real work: on the scale the model is fitted, adjusting for
imbalanced effect modifiers recovers the target's average conditional effect. Parts (b) to (e) are all
about *which effect measure* that recovered number equals. If the reporting scale is collapsible and
aligned with the model (a risk difference), the conditional number is also the marginal policy number (b).
If it is non-collapsible (an odds ratio or hazard ratio), the recovered number is the *conditional* one,
which is a genuinely different quantity from the marginal one, so it must not be read as a marginal odds
ratio (c). If the reporting scale is not even the model scale (a hazard model but an RMST target),
balancing on the model scale need not deliver the target at all (d). And (e) is the one step you cannot
skip: leave an imbalanced effect modifier out of the adjustment set and the estimate is biased. The
roadmap table collects this.

| Part | Condition | What the anchored estimand equals | Plain reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | (i)-(iv), any scale $g$ | target population-average *conditional* effect $\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$ | adjust imbalanced effect modifiers and you recover the conditional effect |
| (b) | aligned $h=g$, collapsible | *also* the target marginal effect | on a risk-difference scale, conditional equals marginal, so you also get the policy number |
| (c) | aligned, *non*-collapsible | the conditional effect, *not* the marginal one | on an odds/hazard-ratio scale you get the conditional measure, not the marginal one |
| (d) | misaligned, $h\circ g^{-1}$ not affine | in general neither, on scale $h$ | a hazard model does not hand you an RMST target for free |
| (e) | an imbalanced effect modifier omitted from $X$ | a biased number | skipping a relevant effect modifier reintroduces the Bucher bias |

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation of the theorem.** If this is an anchored comparison, the operational instruction is
short: adjust for every effect modifier that is imbalanced across the trials and the target, on the scale
you plan to analyze, then read the result as the *conditional* effect on that scale. Do not expect it to
be a marginal odds ratio or hazard ratio unless the estimand and scale conditions of parts (b) to (d) also
line up. Everything else in the theorem is the fine print behind those two sentences. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-anchored-paic-consistency}
## Anchored PAIC consistency (scale-specific)
Consider the anchored two-study setup (@def-pat-setups) targeting population $\mathcal P^{*}$ on model
link $g$. Assume

(i) conditional constancy of relative effects on scale $g$ from each trial population to $\mathcal P^{*}$
(@def-conditional-constancy-relative);

(ii) within-trial identification of the conditional contrasts $\tau^g_{AC}(\cdot),\tau^g_{BC}(\cdot)$
(@thm-g-computation-unbiased);

(iii) every covariate that is an effect modifier on scale $g$ of $A$ versus $C$ or of $B$ versus $C$, and
that is imbalanced between some pair of $\{\mathcal P_{AC},\mathcal P_{BC},\mathcal P^{*}\}$, lies in the
adjustment set $X$ (@def-pat-imbalance);

(iv) overlap: the support of $f_{*}$ on $X$ is contained in the supports of $f_{AC}$ and $f_{BC}$
(@def-positivity).

Then the following hold.

**(a) Conditional recovery, any scale.** The anchored PAIC estimand @eq-pat-anchored-estimand equals the
target population-average conditional effect,
$$
\theta^{\mathrm{anch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})\;=\;\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*}).
$$ {#eq-pat-anchored-cond}

**(b) Marginal recovery on an aligned collapsible scale.** If in addition the reporting scale is aligned,
$h=g$ (@def-scale-alignment), and the effect measure is collapsible on scale $g$ (@def-collapsibility),
and either

  - the measure is *directly* collapsible on $g$ (for instance the identity scale, @prp-emcoll-rd-direct), or
  - the conditional $A$-versus-$B$ contrast $\tau^g_{AB}(\cdot)$ is constant on the support (for instance
    under the shared effect modifier assumption @def-sema),

then the estimand also equals the target *marginal* effect,
$\theta^{\mathrm{anch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})=\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},h}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$.

**(c) The recovered estimand is the conditional effect, not a non-collapsible marginal one.** If the effect measure is non-collapsible on
scale $g$ (the odds ratio on the logit link, the hazard ratio on the log-hazard link,
@thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr), then in general
$\theta^{\mathrm{anch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})\neq\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$, even under
SEMA and scale alignment (@thm-sema-insufficient); only the conditional effect of part (a) is recovered.

**(d) Scale misalignment.** If the reporting scale is misaligned with $h\circ g^{-1}$ not affine (for
instance a hazard model, $g=\log$-hazard, with a restricted mean survival time target, $h$ on the time
scale), then balancing on $g$ does not in general recover the target contrast on $h$, conditional or
marginal.

**(e) Class-wise necessity.** Over the class of data-generating mechanisms in which some covariate is an
effect modifier on scale $g$ and is imbalanced between two of the three populations but is omitted from
$X$, the estimand is asymptotically biased. No claim is made for any specific mechanism: a particular
mechanism may have zero bias by numerical coincidence.

(Corresponds to E.6a to E.6e in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
**(a).** By assumption (ii) the contrasts $\tau^g_{AC}(\cdot)$ and $\tau^g_{BC}(\cdot)$ are identified
within their trials, and by assumption (i) they are the same functions in $\mathcal P^{*}$. By assumption
(iii) every effect modifier that is imbalanced lies in $X$, so each contrast is a function of the adjusted
covariates $X$ alone on the support that matters: any unadjusted covariate $W$ is, by (iii), not an
imbalanced effect modifier, hence either balanced (its conditional distribution given $X$ agrees across the
populations) or not an effect modifier (so @lem-pat-pv-cancellation applies and $W$ drops out of the
contrast). In either case the standardization to $f_{*}$ is governed by the distribution of $X$, and
@prp-pat-conditional-transport gives, for $t\in\{A,B\}$,
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{tC}(\mathcal P^{*})=\int\tau^g_{tC}(x)f_{*}(x)\,dx$, the quantity appearing in
@eq-pat-anchored-estimand, with overlap (iv) ensuring the integral is well defined. Subtracting and
applying the pointwise additivity @lem-pat-conditional-additivity,
$$
\theta^{\mathrm{anch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})
=\int\bigl[\tau^g_{AC}(x)-\tau^g_{BC}(x)\bigr]f_{*}(x)\,dx
=\int\tau^g_{AB}(x)\,f_{*}(x)\,dx
=\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*}),
$$
which is @eq-pat-anchored-cond.

**(b).** By part (a) the estimand equals $\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$. It remains to show
this conditional effect equals the marginal effect $\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},h}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$ under the
stated conditions, on the aligned scale $h=g$. In the first case the measure is directly collapsible on
$g$: by @def-collapsibility the marginal effect equals the population-average conditional effect for every
covariate distribution, so $\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})=\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$
identically, and the conclusion follows; the identity scale is the canonical instance
(@prp-emcoll-rd-direct), giving E.6a. In the second case the conditional contrast $\tau^g_{AB}(\cdot)$ is
constant on the support, say $\tau^g_{AB}(x)\equiv c$; then
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})=\int c\,f_{*}=c$, and collapsibility of the measure
(@def-collapsibility, first bullet) gives that a constant conditional effect equals the marginal effect,
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})=c$; this is the situation of @thm-collapsible-transport, and
with $g=\log$ for the risk ratio it gives E.6b.

**(c).** Suppose the measure is non-collapsible on $g$, and suppose, for contradiction with the generic
claim, that recovery of the marginal effect held for all mechanisms satisfying (i) to (iv) plus SEMA and
alignment. Under SEMA the conditional contrast $\tau^g_{AB}(\cdot)\equiv c$ is constant
(@def-sema below), so part (a) gives $\theta^{\mathrm{anch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})=c$. But non-collapsibility
means precisely that there is a covariate distribution and a pair of stratum means with constant
conditional effect $c$ whose marginal effect differs from $c$ (@def-non-collapsibility,
@thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr): for the odds ratio the marginal effect is strictly attenuated toward the
null. Hence $\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})\neq c=\theta^{\mathrm{anch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$
for such a mechanism, contradicting universal recovery. The "if and only if" of @thm-sema-insufficient
makes this sharp: under SEMA and alignment, direct transportability of the marginal effect holds for all
populations if and only if the measure is collapsible. Thus only the conditional effect is recovered in
general.

**(d).** Write $h=H\circ g$ with $H=h\circ g^{-1}$ not affine. (An affine $H$ only rescales and shifts
the $g$ scale, and then the $h$-contrast is a fixed multiple of the $g$-contrast.) Part (a)
recovers the $g$-scale conditional contrast $\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$. The target on
the reporting scale is built from the $h$-scale conditional means $h(\mu_t(x))=H(g(\mu_t(x)))$, and because
$H$ is nonlinear the $h$-scale conditional contrast $h(\mu_B(x))-h(\mu_A(x))$ is not a function of the
$g$-scale contrast $g(\mu_B(x))-g(\mu_A(x))$ alone; it depends separately on the baseline $g(\mu_A(x))$.
Transporting the $g$-scale contrast therefore does not determine the $h$-scale contrast, conditional or
marginal. The survival instance, where $g$ is the log-hazard and $h$ encodes the restricted mean survival
time through the nonlinear functional $\mathrm{RMST}_t(\tau\mid x)=\int_0^\tau\exp\!\bigl(-\int_0^u h_t(s\mid x)\,ds\bigr)du$
of the hazard, is E.6e; we defer its survival-specific development to the later chapters on general
likelihoods and ML-UMR, and record here only that the obstruction is exactly the nonlinearity of $H$.

**(e).** Suppose a covariate $W$ is an effect modifier on $g$ of, say, $A$ versus $C$, and is imbalanced
between $\mathcal P_{AC}$ and $\mathcal P^{*}$, but is omitted from $X$. Then the standardization in part
(a) computes, for the $AC$ contrast, $\int\tau^g_{AC}(x,w)\,f^{AC}(w\mid x)\,f_{*}(x)\,dx\,dw$ rather than
the target $\int\tau^g_{AC}(x,w)\,f^{*}(w\mid x)\,f_{*}(x)\,dx\,dw$, and the difference is the failure-of-Bucher
residual of @thm-failure-of-bucher,
$$
\theta^{\mathrm{anch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})-\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},g}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})
=\int\tau^g_{AC}(x,w)\,[\,f^{AC}(w\mid x)-f^{*}(w\mid x)\,]\,f_{*}(x)\,dx\,dw,
$$
which by @thm-failure-of-bucher(2) is nonzero for some mechanism in the stated class, since $\tau^g_{AC}$
depends nontrivially on $w$ (effect modification) and the conditional distributions of $W$ differ
(imbalance). The statement is class-wise: by @thm-failure-of-bucher(1) the residual vanishes identically
only when the modifier is balanced or absent, but a specific mechanism may zero the integral by
cancellation even with an unadjusted imbalanced modifier. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Where the comparator earns its keep.** Part (a) is the engine; parts (b) to (e) are about which scale the
engine's output lives on. The reason the anchored estimand needs only effect modifiers in $X$, and not all
prognostic variables, is @lem-pat-pv-cancellation: a purely prognostic $W$ enters $\tau^g_{AC}$ and
$\tau^g_{BC}$ only through the comparator term $g(\mu_C(x,w))$, which is the same in both and cancels in the
contrast. This is the conditional-level descendant of the baseline cancellation
(@prp-baseline-cancellation) that made anchored comparison robust in Chapter 14. The unanchored case
forfeits exactly this cancellation. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** Part (a) is population adjustment stated as a regression fact: it is standardization,
the same operation that turns a fitted outcome model into a marginal prediction in Chapter 10, now aimed at
a *different* population than the one that supplied the data. The anchored theorem is the formal license
for the whole of Part IV. It says the effect-modifier bookkeeping that broke Bucher in Chapter 16 is fully
repaired by adjusting the imbalanced modifiers, and it pins down the estimand each downstream method (MAIC,
STC, ML-NMR) may claim. In the anticoagulant example, part (a) promises that adjusting for age turns the
biased Bucher answer of Step 3 in @exm-pat-anchored into the exact target risk difference of Step 4, while
part (c) warns that the same adjustment on the odds-ratio scale returns only the conditional odds ratio,
not the marginal one a reimbursement dossier may quote. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

For completeness we record the finite, exact algebraic identity underlying part (a) in the form proved in
the Coq development: once the adjusted $AC$ contrast has been correctly identified in the target and the
AgD $BC$ contrast is unbiased, the Bucher subtraction returns the target contrast.

::: {#cor-pat-anchored-algebra}
## The adjusted Bucher identity
Let $\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{adj}}$ be an estimator of the target $A$-versus-$C$ contrast with
$\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{adj}}=d_{AC(\mathcal P^{*})}$, let $\hat d_{BC}$ satisfy $\hat d_{BC}=d_{BC(\mathcal P^{*})}$,
and let transitivity hold in $\mathcal P^{*}$ in the form $d_{AB(\mathcal P^{*})}=d_{AC(\mathcal P^{*})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P^{*})}$.
Then $\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{adj}}-\hat d_{BC}=d_{AB(\mathcal P^{*})}$.
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/EffectModifiers.v`, `Theorem anchored_unbiased`]

::: {.proof}
Substitute the two identifications and the transitivity relation:
$\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{adj}}-\hat d_{BC}=d_{AC(\mathcal P^{*})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P^{*})}=d_{AB(\mathcal P^{*})}$.
$\square$
:::

## The unanchored consistency theorem {#sec-pat-unanchored}

Without a comparator, the estimator must transport each absolute marginal mean separately, and there is no
cancellation to relieve it of the prognostic variables.

The unanchored setup is a method of last resort, and it helps to know when a health researcher is forced
into it. It arises when the two treatments were never controlled against a common arm: perhaps $A$ was
licensed on a single-arm study, common for accelerated approvals in oncology and rare disease, while $B$
comes from a placebo-controlled trial, so there is no shared placebo or active comparator to difference
against. Stripped of the comparator, the estimator can no longer content itself with contrasts; it must
rebuild each arm's absolute outcome in the target population and only then take a difference. That is why
the assumptions jump from relative to absolute constancy and from effect modifiers to all prognostic
variables.

Define the **unanchored PAIC estimand** at target
$\mathcal P^{*}$ on reporting scale $h$ as
$$
\theta^{\mathrm{unanch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})\;:=\;h\!\left(m_B(\mathcal P^{*})\right)-h\!\left(m_A(\mathcal P^{*})\right)
\;=\;\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},h}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*}),
$$ {#eq-pat-unanchored-estimand}
with $m_t(\mathcal P^{*})=\int\mu_t(x)f_{*}(x)\,dx$ as in @eq-pat-marginal-mean.

::: {#thm-unanchored-paic-consistency}
## Unanchored PAIC consistency
Consider the unanchored two-study setup (@def-pat-setups) targeting $\mathcal P^{*}$ on reporting scale
$h$. Assume

(i) conditional constancy of **absolute** effects (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute): the conditional
mean function $\mu_t(\cdot)$ is the same in each source and in $\mathcal P^{*}$;

(ii) within-trial identification of $\mu_A(\cdot)$ and $\mu_B(\cdot)$ (@thm-g-computation-unbiased);

(iii) every covariate that is **either** an effect modifier on the modeled scale **or** a prognostic
variable for $A$ or $B$, and that is imbalanced between some pair of the source and target populations,
lies in the adjustment set $X$;

(iv) overlap (@def-positivity).

Then the unanchored PAIC estimand @eq-pat-unanchored-estimand is recovered: each marginal mean is
identified by the transport g-formula,
$$
m_t(\mathcal P^{*})\;=\;\int\mu_t(x)\,f_{*}(x)\,dx
\;=\;\mathbb E_{X\sim\mathcal P_{\mathrm{src},t}}\!\left[\,w_t(X)\,\mu_t(X)\,\right],\qquad
w_t(x)=\frac{f_{*}(x)}{f_{\mathrm{src},t}(x)},
$$ {#eq-pat-unanchored-recovery}
and applying $h$ and differencing gives $\theta^{\mathrm{unanch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})=\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},h}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})$.

**Necessity (over a class).** Over the class of mechanisms with an imbalanced prognostic variable for $A$
or $B$ omitted from $X$, the estimand is asymptotically biased, with bias for the $A$ arm
$$
\int\!\!\int\mu_A(x,w)\,[\,f_{\mathrm{src},A}(w\mid x)-f^{*}(w\mid x)\,]\,f_{*}(x)\,dw\,dx,
$$ {#eq-pat-unanchored-bias}
which is nonzero whenever $\mu_A$ depends on the omitted $w$ (prognostic) and its conditional distribution
differs between source and target (imbalance), with no comparator term to cancel it.

(Corresponds to E.7 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
By assumption (ii) the function $\mu_t(\cdot)$ is identified within its source, and by (i) it is the same
function in $\mathcal P^{*}$. By (iii) every imbalanced prognostic variable lies in $X$, so on the relevant
support $\mu_t$ is a function of $X$ alone: any omitted covariate is either balanced, with the same
conditional distribution given $X$ in source and target, or nonprognostic, in which case it does not enter
$\mu_t$. Applying the transport g-formula @thm-conditional-transportability to the function $\mu_t$ gives
@eq-pat-unanchored-recovery, with overlap (iv) guaranteeing the integral and the reweighting are well
defined. Both arms are handled this way; there is no subtraction step, so the two transports are
independent. Applying $h$ to the two recovered marginal means and differencing yields
$\theta^{\mathrm{unanch}}_{AB}(\mathcal P^{*})=h(m_B(\mathcal P^{*}))-h(m_A(\mathcal P^{*}))$, which is the
target marginal effect.

For the necessity claim, let $W$ be prognostic for $A$ and imbalanced, but omitted from $X$. The estimator
that adjusts only on $X$ computes the source within-stratum average
$\bar\mu_A^{\mathrm{src}}(x)=\int\mu_A(x,w)f_{\mathrm{src},A}(w\mid x)\,dw$ and standardizes it to $f_{*}$,
producing $\int\bar\mu_A^{\mathrm{src}}(x)f_{*}(x)\,dx$. The target requires the target within-stratum
average $\bar\mu_A^{*}(x)=\int\mu_A(x,w)f^{*}(w\mid x)\,dw$, so the bias of the $A$ marginal mean is
$\int[\bar\mu_A^{\mathrm{src}}(x)-\bar\mu_A^{*}(x)]f_{*}(x)\,dx$, which is @eq-pat-unanchored-bias. Because
$\mu_A$ depends on $w$ and the conditional laws of $W$ differ, the inner difference is generically nonzero,
and there is no comparator arm whose identical bias would cancel it in a contrast. By contrast, in the
anchored case the analogous term enters through the comparator and cancels (@lem-pat-pv-cancellation), which
is precisely why a purely prognostic imbalance is harmless there and harmful here. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation, and the shared prognostic factor assumption.** The instruction for an unanchored
comparison is the anchored one with the safety catch removed: adjust for every imbalanced covariate that
predicts the outcome, whether or not it modifies any treatment effect. In the model @eq-pat-nmr the
matching structural hypothesis is that the covariate-outcome slopes are the same under the compared
treatments, the **shared prognostic factor assumption** (SPFA) of [Notation](/notation.qmd), used by ML-UMR
in Chapter 26. As a slope restriction SPFA coincides with SEMA; what makes the unanchored comparison harder
to defend is that it must be paired with absolute rather than relative constancy (@prp-spfa-vs-sema). The practical reading of overlap here is the one
that should worry a health researcher: the target population must not contain patient profiles the source
never enrolled, because the weight $w_t(x)=f_{*}(x)/f_{\mathrm{src},t}(x)$ is undefined where the source
density is zero. If the target has sicker patients than any trial subject, the method is extrapolating,
not transporting, and the guarantee lapses. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The price of dropping the anchor.** The anchored theorem asked for effect modifiers in $X$; the
unanchored theorem asks for effect modifiers *and* prognostic variables. By @lem-pat-em-not-pv the second
demand is strictly stronger: a covariate can be prognostic without modifying any contrast, and such a
covariate is invisible to the anchored adjustment but must be measured and balanced for the unanchored one.
In practice this is close to prohibitive, because it requires having measured essentially every driver of
the outcome. This is the formal reason that unanchored comparison is a method of last resort, reserved for
disconnected networks (Chapter 26), and that @phillippo2016tsd18 demands extensive sensitivity analysis
whenever it is used. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Non-collapsibility, again.** Equation @eq-pat-unanchored-recovery recovers the marginal means $m_t$
themselves, so for a non-collapsible reporting scale the unanchored estimand is the genuine marginal
effect in $\mathcal P^{*}$, not merely a conditional one. The subtlety of part (c) of the anchored theorem
does not arise here, because nothing was differenced before applying $h$. What does carry over is that the
recovered marginal effect is specific to $\mathcal P^{*}$: a non-collapsible marginal effect computed for
one target does not transport unchanged to another, exactly as in @thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr. The
untestability of the absolute-constancy assumption (i) is taken up in @prp-testable-untestable-constancy.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The shared effect modifier assumption {#sec-pat-sema}

The anchored theorem assumed the conditional contrasts $\tau^g_{AC}$ and $\tau^g_{BC}$ were both available.
In the smallest network, one IPD trial of $A$ versus $C$ and one AgD trial of $B$ versus $C$, the IPD
identifies the interactions for $A$ but the AgD cannot identify the interactions for $B$ separately from
its main effect. The assumption that restores identifiability is that the active treatments share their
effect-modifier structure.

::: {#def-sema}
## Shared effect modifier assumption (SEMA)
In the model @eq-pat-nmr, the **shared effect modifier assumption** asserts that the treatment-by-covariate
interactions are the same for the active treatments being compared:
$$
\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}\;=\;\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\;=:\;\boldsymbol\beta_{2}.
$$ {#eq-pat-sema}
(Corresponds to E.8 in the proof catalogue.) $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation: what SEMA says, and how it differs from conditional constancy.** SEMA says the
covariates bend the two active treatments' effects *in the same way*. In the anticoagulant example it asks
that age change the benefit of the new drug $A$ versus warfarin by exactly the amount it changes the
benefit of the DOAC $B$ versus warfarin, so that when we difference $A$ against $B$ the age term cancels
and the $A$-versus-$B$ effect stops depending on age. Contrast this with conditional constancy
(@def-conditional-constancy-relative), which is an assumption *across populations*, the same effect
function in every trial and the target; SEMA is an assumption *across treatments within one model*, the
same interaction vector for $A$ and $B$. One is portability of a fixed effect to a new patient mix; the
other is a shared shape of effect modification between two drugs.

A plausible instance: $A$ and $B$ are two drugs of the same pharmacological class and the only strong
modifier is disease severity, which blunts any active treatment's advantage over the comparator by a
similar amount, so severity modifies $A$-versus-$C$ and $B$-versus-$C$ alike and cancels. An implausible
instance: $A$ is a targeted therapy whose benefit is concentrated in a biomarker-positive subgroup while
$B$ is a broad-acting comparator whose benefit is flat across that biomarker; then the biomarker modifies
$A$ but not $B$, SEMA fails, and the active-versus-active contrast genuinely depends on the biomarker mix.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#prp-pat-sema-constant}
## SEMA makes the active-versus-active conditional contrast constant
Under the model @eq-pat-nmr and SEMA (@def-sema), the conditional effect of $A$ versus $B$ on scale $g$ is
constant in $x$:
$$
\tau^g_{AB}(x)\;=\;\gamma_B-\gamma_A\qquad\text{for all }x .
$$ {#eq-pat-sema-constant}
:::

::: {.proof}
By @eq-pat-tau-linear, $\tau^g_{AC}(x)=-(\gamma_A+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}^\top x)$ and
$\tau^g_{BC}(x)=-(\gamma_B+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}^\top x)$. By @lem-pat-conditional-additivity,
$$
\tau^g_{AB}(x)=\tau^g_{AC}(x)-\tau^g_{BC}(x)
=(\gamma_B-\gamma_A)+(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A})^\top x .
$$
SEMA @eq-pat-sema sets the interaction difference to zero, leaving the constant $\gamma_B-\gamma_A$.
$\square$
:::

@prp-pat-sema-constant is what links SEMA to part (b) of the anchored theorem: with the
active-versus-active conditional contrast constant, a *collapsible* aligned reporting scale recovers the
marginal effect (@thm-collapsible-transport), whereas a *non-collapsible* one still does not
(@thm-sema-insufficient). SEMA buys identifiability on the linear-predictor scale; it does not by itself
buy transportability of a non-collapsible marginal effect.

::: {#thm-shared-em-identifiability}
## Identifiability under SEMA in the smallest network
Consider one IPD trial on $\{A,C\}$ in $\mathcal P_{AC}$ and one AgD trial on $\{B,C\}$ in
$\mathcal P_{BC}$, modeled by @eq-pat-nmr under SEMA (@def-sema). Suppose the IPD design has full column
rank (both arms present and the covariates have nondegenerate within-arm variation) and the AgD reports its
$B$-versus-$C$ average conditional contrast on scale $g$ together with the covariate mean $\bar x_{BC}$
(on a collapsible scale this is the reported marginal contrast; the non-collapsible case, where the AgD
trial reports only a marginal contrast, is handled by integration in Chapter 23). Then the
target-population linear-predictor contrast $\gamma_B-\gamma_A$ is identified from the combined
IPD-plus-AgD likelihood. (Corresponds to E.9 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
From the IPD trial, the conditional mean model @eq-pat-nmr restricted to arms $A$ and $C$ is a generalized
linear model with linear predictor $\mu_{AC}+\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top x$ on the $C$ arm and
$\mu_{AC}+\gamma_A+(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2})^\top x$ on the $A$ arm. With full column rank
of the design and a strictly monotone link, the coefficients of a generalized linear model are identified
(Chapter 7), meaning the map from coefficients to the fitted conditional means is injective, so that no two
distinct coefficient vectors produce the same fit: the $C$ arm identifies $(\mu_{AC},\boldsymbol\beta_1)$,
and the $A$ arm then identifies
$(\gamma_A,\boldsymbol\beta_{2})$. In particular the shared interaction vector $\boldsymbol\beta_{2}$ is
known from the IPD.

From the AgD trial, the reported $B$-versus-$C$ average conditional contrast on scale $g$ is, by
@eq-pat-trial-contrast and the linear form @eq-pat-tau-linear under SEMA,
$$
\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=-\int\bigl(\gamma_B+\boldsymbol\beta_{2}^\top x\bigr)f_{BC}(x)\,dx
=-\bigl(\gamma_B+\boldsymbol\beta_{2}^\top\bar x_{BC}\bigr),
$$
a single linear equation in the one unknown $\gamma_B$, since $\boldsymbol\beta_{2}$ is known from the IPD
and $\bar x_{BC}$ is reported. Solving, $\gamma_B=-\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2}^\top\bar x_{BC}$,
so $\gamma_B$ is identified. Hence $\gamma_B-\gamma_A$ is identified from the joint data. The network is
connected through the shared comparator $C$, so the rank condition for network identifiability
(@thm-fe-nma-identifiability) is met trivially. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What identifiability does and does not give.** @thm-shared-em-identifiability identifies the
contrast on the linear-predictor scale $g$. It does **not** identify a marginal effect on a non-collapsible
reporting scale: that requires the joint covariate distribution and the baseline risk of the target,
through the non-collapsibility of @thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr, and is governed by part (c) of
@thm-anchored-paic-consistency and by @thm-sema-insufficient. This is the same caveat that recurs whenever
the odds ratio or hazard ratio is the quoted measure. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Scale dependence of effect modifier status {#sec-pat-scale-dep}

The conditions of the consistency theorems are stated "on scale $g$," and the qualifier is not decorative:
whether a covariate is an effect modifier can change with the scale. The following worked counterexample,
with arithmetic the reader can check by hand, exhibits a covariate that modifies the effect on the logit
scale but not on the risk-difference scale.

::: {#exm-scale-dependence-em}
## A covariate that is an effect modifier on the logit scale but not the identity scale
Let $X\in\{0,1\}$ be binary, let treatment be $t\in\{0,1\}$, and let the outcome be binary with conditional
risks
$$
\mu_0(0)=0.1,\quad \mu_1(0)=0.2,\quad \mu_0(1)=0.5,\quad \mu_1(1)=0.6 .
$$

**Risk-difference (identity) scale.** The conditional risk differences are
$$
\tau^{\mathrm{id}}(0)=\mu_1(0)-\mu_0(0)=0.2-0.1=0.1,\qquad
\tau^{\mathrm{id}}(1)=\mu_1(1)-\mu_0(1)=0.6-0.5=0.1 .
$$
They are equal, so the conditional risk difference does not depend on $x$: by @def-effect-modifier, $X$ is
**not** an effect modifier on the identity scale.

**Log-odds-ratio (logit) scale.** The conditional log odds ratios are
$$
\tau^{\mathrm{logit}}(0)=\operatorname{logit}(0.2)-\operatorname{logit}(0.1)
=\log\tfrac{0.2/0.8}{0.1/0.9}=\log 2.25\approx 0.8109,
$$
$$
\tau^{\mathrm{logit}}(1)=\operatorname{logit}(0.6)-\operatorname{logit}(0.5)
=\log\tfrac{0.6/0.4}{0.5/0.5}=\log 1.5\approx 0.4055 .
$$
They differ, so by @def-effect-modifier, $X$ **is** an effect modifier on the logit scale.

(Corresponds to E.10 in the proof catalogue.) $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Consequences for practice.** The example shows that "$X$ is not an effect modifier," and therefore the
entire question "which covariates must be in the adjustment set," is meaningless until the scale is named.
A SEMA that holds on the identity scale need not hold on the logit scale, and the adjustment that licenses
an anchored mean-difference comparison need not license an anchored odds-ratio comparison. This is the
finite, concrete face of the scale specificity that makes the older scale-free "iff" formulations
untenable, and it is why @thm-anchored-paic-consistency is stated one scale at a time. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Testable and untestable parts of constancy {#sec-pat-testable}

The constancy assumptions E.4, E.5, and SEMA are the load-bearing hypotheses of population adjustment, and
it is natural to ask whether the data can check them. The answer divides sharply by network size.

The short answer, and the single most important practical message of the chapter, is that in a two-study
comparison these assumptions **cannot be checked from the data at all**; they must be argued from external
knowledge. The reason is a counting mismatch. The AgD trial hands us exactly one number about treatment
$B$'s effect modification, a single average contrast at a single covariate mean, but the interactions we
would need to verify are a whole vector, one coefficient per covariate. One number cannot pin down a
vector. Geometrically, that one equation carves out a flat hyperplane of
$(\gamma_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})$ pairs that all reproduce the observed summary; SEMA picks one point on
that hyperplane, the point where $B$'s interactions match $A$'s, and nothing in the data says whether that
point is the right one. The proposition makes this precise.

::: {#prp-testable-untestable-constancy}
## Testability of the shared effect modifier assumption
In the smallest anchored network of @thm-shared-em-identifiability (one IPD trial on $\{A,C\}$, one AgD
trial on $\{B,C\}$), SEMA (@def-sema) imposes no restriction on the observable data distribution: the SEMA
model and the unrestricted model with $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\neq\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}$ fit the observed
summaries identically. Hence SEMA is untestable from these data. If instead a second AgD trial on
$\{B,C\}$ is available at a covariate mean $\bar x_{BC}'\neq\bar x_{BC}$, then SEMA implies the
over-identifying restriction
$$
\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC}')}\;=\;-\boldsymbol\beta_{2}^\top\bigl(\bar x_{BC}-\bar x_{BC}'\bigr),
$$ {#eq-pat-overid}
and is therefore testable on the covariate directions spanned by $\bar x_{BC}-\bar x_{BC}'$. (Corresponds
to E.11 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
From the AgD trial the only functional of the $B$-versus-$C$ interactions that enters the likelihood is the
scalar $\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=-(\gamma_B+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}^\top\bar x_{BC})$ (the average
conditional contrast at the reported covariate mean). Given the IPD, which fixes $\boldsymbol\beta_{2}$ and
the remaining parameters, the set of $(\gamma_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})$ consistent with the AgD is the
entire hyperplane $\{(\gamma_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}):\gamma_B+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}^\top\bar x_{BC}=-\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}\}$.
The SEMA point $(\,-\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2}^\top\bar x_{BC},\ \boldsymbol\beta_{2}\,)$
lies on this hyperplane, but so does every other point; all give the same observable summary. Therefore no
function of the data distinguishes the SEMA model from an unrestricted one, and SEMA is untestable. The
target contrast $\gamma_B-\gamma_A$ does depend on which point of the hyperplane is selected, which is why
SEMA is simultaneously necessary for identification and beyond the reach of the data.

With a second AgD trial at $\bar x_{BC}'$ the data deliver a second scalar
$\tilde d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC}')}=-(\gamma_B+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}^\top\bar x_{BC}')$. Under SEMA both must be
explained by the single, IPD-fixed $\boldsymbol\beta_{2}$, so their difference must equal
$-\boldsymbol\beta_{2}^\top(\bar x_{BC}-\bar x_{BC}')$; any departure of the observed difference from this
predicted value falsifies SEMA on the spanned direction. This is the over-identifying restriction
@eq-pat-overid, and it is the node-splitting logic of @def-node-splitting specialized to the regression
coefficients. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The general principle.** Conditional constancy of relative effects (E.4) and of absolute effects (E.5)
are likewise testable only when the network carries direct and indirect evidence for the same contrast, so
that the consistency equation provides an over-identifying restriction (node-splitting,
@def-node-splitting). In the two-study PAIC setting the model is just-identified for the target contrast,
no restriction remains, and the assumptions must be defended by domain knowledge: pharmacological
similarity of $A$ and $B$, mechanistic argument, and sensitivity analysis over plausible violations. This
is the methodological warning of @phillippo2016tsd18. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Target-population estimands via the g-formula {#sec-pat-estimands}

We close the abstract development by pinning down the estimands the methods target, and the precise sense
in which they are identified. Both are g-formula functionals of the conditional means and the target
covariate distribution; they connect this chapter to the transportability theory of Chapter 12. Much of
this theorem's content has appeared piecemeal above; the value of stating it once is that it is the clean
summary of *what* is identified and *when* the two estimands coincide, and it is the statement the method
chapters cite.

::: {#thm-target-population-estimand}
## Target-population estimands and their identification
Fix a target population $\mathcal P^{*}$ and a reporting scale $h$. Define the **target marginal effect**
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},h}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})=h\!\left(\textstyle\int\mu_b(x)f_{*}(x)\,dx\right)-h\!\left(\textstyle\int\mu_a(x)f_{*}(x)\,dx\right)
$$ {#eq-pat-target-marg}
and the **target population-average conditional effect**
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},h}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})=\int\bigl[h(\mu_b(x))-h(\mu_a(x))\bigr]f_{*}(x)\,dx .
$$ {#eq-pat-target-cond}
Assume within-trial identification (@thm-g-computation-unbiased), the relevant constancy assumption
(@def-conditional-constancy-relative for a contrast, or @def-conditional-constancy-absolute for the
separate arms), and overlap (@def-positivity). Then:

**(a) Identification.** Both estimands are identified from the source conditional means and the target
covariate distribution, by the transport g-formula (@thm-conditional-transportability): @eq-pat-target-marg
applies the formula to each $\mu_t$, and @eq-pat-target-cond applies it to the function $x\mapsto h(\mu_b(x))-h(\mu_a(x))$.

**(b) Coincidence under collapsibility.** If $h$ is directly collapsible on its scale (the identity scale,
@prp-emcoll-rd-direct), or if $h$ is collapsible and the conditional contrast is constant on the support
(the log risk ratio on the log scale, @thm-collapsible-transport), then
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg},h}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})=\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond},h}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})$.

**(c) Divergence under non-collapsibility.** If $h$ is non-collapsible (logit, log-hazard), the two
estimands differ in general (@thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr), and the marginal estimand depends on the target
baseline risk, not only on the transported contrast.

(Corresponds to E.12 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
**(a).** By within-trial identification and the relevant constancy assumption, the conditional means
$\mu_t(\cdot)$ (for the unanchored or marginal target) or the conditional contrasts $\tau^h_{ab}(\cdot)$
(for the conditional target) are population-free functions identified from the source. The transport
g-formula @thm-conditional-transportability identifies the expectation under $f_{*}$ of any such fixed
function of $x$: applied to $\mu_b$ and $\mu_a$ it yields the two marginal means $m_b(\mathcal P^{*})$ and
$m_a(\mathcal P^{*})$, and applying $h$ and differencing gives @eq-pat-target-marg; applied to the function
$h(\mu_b(\cdot))-h(\mu_a(\cdot))$ it yields @eq-pat-target-cond directly. Overlap guarantees the integrals
are well defined.

**(b).** Direct collapsibility means, by @def-collapsibility, that the marginal effect equals the
population-average conditional effect for every covariate distribution. On the identity scale this is
@prp-emcoll-rd-direct; for the log risk ratio with a constant conditional contrast it is the collapsibility
